newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat visits Israel, makes anti-violence pledge.
newsitem.headline: Arafat visits Israel, makes anti-violence pledge.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat paid a confidence-building visit to Israel on Tuesday, pledging to pursue peace without resorting to violence.

Two weeks after Israelis and Palestinians were locked in bloody clashes in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Arab East Jerusalem, an Israeli air force helicopter flew Arafat to President Ezer Weizman's home for a burying of the hatchet.
A beaming Arafat, on his first public visit to Israel, struck all the right chords in a country shaken by the sight of Palestinian policemen exchanging fire with Israeli soldiers.
"Negotiations will be the tool to resolve our differences," Arafat told a news conference after a 25-minute meeting with Weizman, whose post is largely ceremonial.
Asked whether Palestinian police would no longer fire at Israeli troops, he replied: "This is my permanent order to our policemen."

Arafat's visit was another indication Israel and the PLO had pulled back from the brink after gunbattles last month, touched off by Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy places in Jerusalem, killed 59 Palestinians and 15 Jews.

His wide smiles were in stark contrast to the gloomy image he projected in appearances before the media during an emergency White House summit last week with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"We are determined to continue with this road of a new Middle East that will be devoid of wars, violence and counter-violence for the sake of cousins, friends and brothers," Arafat said.
Weizman said he and Arafat spoke about "the recent tragedy of gunfire, losses on both sides and we decided this kind of thing cannot happen again".

Unlike the right-wing Netanyahu, Weizman is viewed by many Arabs as a peacemaker -- although at the height of Moslem suicide bombings in February and March the president called for a slowing of the Israel-PLO peace process.
Weizman, defence minister in the Likud government of the late prime minister Menachem Begin, was an architect of the 1979 Israeli-Egyptian peace treaty.
Two months ago, Weizman -- a former combat pilot with a reputation for shooting straight from the lip -- embarrassed Netanyahu by saying he would meet Arafat if the prime minister would not.
Netanyahu has since met Arafat once in Gaza and again in Washington.

The Palestinian leader's only previous visit to Israel -- at night and without advance announcement -- was a condolence call on the widow of assassinated prime minister Yitzhak Rabin last November in Tel Aviv.
Weizman has met Arafat twice, in 1994 at the inauguration of South African President Nelson Mandela and last January at the funeral of French President Francois Mitterrand.
By hosting Arafat at his private residence, rather than at his official office in Jerusalem, Weizman avoided the political uproar that a visit to the holy city would have triggered among Israelis.
Arafat was due to return to Gaza after meeting Weizman.
